As stated above, to maintain open access principles and not negatively impact generation projects that are already in the queue, BYOG arrangements must be electrically close, if not behind the same POI, then at least in the same zone.

The Commission should instead require transmission providers to develop methodologies that allocate ancillary service and transmission costs in proportion to the level of service and reliability actually used by each customer.
The Commission should also make explicit that BYOG arrangements may include Distributed Energy Resource Aggregations (sometimes referred to as 'Virtual Power Plants' (VPPs)).

letters.desc: UCS accepts the concept of net-based injection and withdrawal rights for hybrid facilities but argues the study process must still separately evaluate gross load and gross generation amounts. Power limiting systems are not instantaneous, so relying on net rights alone understates the range of grid impacts a hybrid facility can cause. Rules must be grounded in explicit, measurable performance standards.
quotes: capabilities to limit injections or withdrawals are not instantaneous and are not error-proof.
the full nameplate capacity must still be used when studying fault conditions to identify power quality impacts.

the drafting and adoption of rules that presume tight control and a narrow range of performance from conventional generation with co-located loads will need to be based on clearly stated and explicitly measured standards or limits.

system protection facilities must: 1. Ensure that if the facility exceeds the allowed limits, its import or export is returned to the allowed limits within a fixed time period, defined by the TSO. 2. During the inadvertent export or import event, maintain the voltage at the point of interconnection within limits defined by the TSO.

letters.desc: Vantage raises two concerns about full dispatchability of hybrid generation: it undermines the reliability rationale for on-site generation if dispatched power cannot be instantly recalled during a grid outage, and it may subject hybrid generation owners to FERC public utility regulation under FPA Section 201(e).
quotes: making the generation associated with hybrid facilities fully dispatchable (even if restricted only to grid emergencies) undermines the reliability rationale for installing that generation in the first place.

traditional contractual and organized market rule structures for dispatchability may subject the owner or operator of the hybrid facility's generation to Commission regulation as a statutory public utility under Section 201(e) of the Federal Power Act.

letters.org: Wisconsin Electric Power CompanyWisconsin Public Service Corporation
letters.desc: WEC warns that co-located generation selling to an adjacent load is a retail sale beyond FERC's jurisdiction. If the Commission proceeds, it must restrict withdrawal and injection to each facility's entitlements and cannot allow co-located arrangements to bypass state franchise laws.
quotes: A generation facility that is co-located with a large load and which then sells its energy product to that load is, by definition, making a retail sale.  This is true regardless of whether the co-located load is interconnected at the transmission level or at distribution voltage.  Commission regulation of this retail sale would extend far beyond regulating interconnections as a "component" or "element" of transmission service and would clearly be ultra vires.

the Commission should make the "gross" amount of load the default approach for studying large load interconnections consistent with existing Commission precedent.  This will ensure that co-located arrangements are appropriately studied based on their actual use of the transmission system, even if the load or generation has its withdrawal or injection rights based on the net capacity behind the meter.

If the net withdrawal or injection of co-located facilities are permitted to influence transmission cost allocation, the Commission should ensure that there are adequate restrictions on the ability of the load or generation facility to withdraw or inject beyond their respective entitlements.

any rulemaking should ensure that franchised service territories are protected and that any processes mandated by a rule does not permit generators to serve co-located load in violation of retail franchise laws.

letters.desc: AEMA argues that proposals requiring every large load to bring its own generation ignore the efficiency of the transmission grid and would raise costs and delay projects without adding reliability benefits that demand flexibility cannot already provide. A final rule limiting expedited treatment to generation-paired loads would be unduly discriminatory.
quotes: AEMA strongly urges the Commission to reject arguments from the Independent Market Monitor for PJM ("PJM IMM"), the Electric Power Supply Association ("EPSA"), the Illinois Attorney General, and others suggesting that large loads must "bring their own generation" or that demand-side solutions are inferior to generation assets.

Mandating that every new large load be paired with new generation forces the construction of redundant capital assets when cost-effective flexibility could otherwise allow that load to be served by the existing system. This approach would unnecessarily inflate the cost of AI infrastructure and add years of supply chain backlog.
AEMA urges the Commission to treat generation matching as one optional pathway among many to achieve flexibility, not as a mandatory precondition for timely interconnection.

a final rule singling out loads or hybrid facilities that pair matching generation as the sole mechanism for expedited interconnection—while excluding verifiable load flexibility—would be unduly discriminatory.

letters.desc: The Alliance opposes any rule that gives queue priority to co-located or hybrid facilities, since the additional design and financing costs of hybrid projects fall more heavily on Tribal developers. It asks the Commission to limit the net withdrawal/injection provision to its technical calculation function without affecting queue order.
quotes: Prioritizing large load interconnection applicants in the queue based on whether they are co-located with generation creates a market where hybrid facilities may be more competitive than non-hybrid facilities.

We call on the Commission to clarify that this proposed rule only allows the calculation of net withdrawal/injection rights and does not impact the order of prioritization in the interconnection queue.

letters.desc: The filer argues that large load customers are not analogous to generation owners and should not receive an equivalent option to build interconnection facilities. Extending that right to data centers and industrial customers without grid expertise creates reliability risk.
quotes: large load customers should not be entitled to the same option to build as generation owners.

letters.desc: Duke Energy opposes a proximity-based hybrid facility definition, insisting load and generation must be behind a common point of interconnection. It also insists providers must study full operating ranges, not just net contractual rights, to avoid unstudied reliability conditions.
quotes: Duke Energy strongly recommends that any definition of 'hybrid facilities' require that the load and generation be behind a common point of interconnection to the transmission system.
'Nearness' of load and generation is not a technically implementable standard, and the 'nearness' of load and generation does not determine the electrical impacts to the transmission system.
Transmission providers must have the ability to study all load and generation, including hybrid facilities, in a manner that reflects the potential actual operating impacts to the grid.

letters.desc: EPSA opposes the view that any hybrid load interconnection must include a delivery meter. Requiring such a meter would treat every hybrid connection as a state-jurisdictional arrangement and give transmission owners unwarranted control over federal interconnection.
quotes: This hook is also inappropriately established by comments suggesting that any hybrid load interconnection must include a delivery meter – thereby transmogrifying every connection into a state-jurisdictional arrangement.

letters.desc: Entergy opposes studying hybrid facilities on a net injection or withdrawal basis, warning that net-basis studies miss large actual load flows, underidentify needed upgrades, and create reliability risks from variable generator output and withdrawal patterns.
quotes: It would be overly simplistic to assume that a hybrid load's net injection or withdrawal impacts on the grid will be constant over any period of time.  Reliability issues can arise if a study of a hybrid facility assumes a certain level of energy injections onto the grid, but injections in fact exceed that level, or if no withdrawal rights are assumed but withdrawals occur.

netting should not affect the way an interconnection request is studied.  Studying hybrid facilities in the manner contemplated by the proposed ANOPR may fail to identify needed network upgrades, because it will be blind to potentially substantial new loads, as long as those new loads are 'hybrid.'

letters.desc: Entergy contends that studying hybrid facilities on a net-injection basis alone creates reliability risks by ignoring peak gross demand when co-located generation is unavailable. It also warns that broadening the hybrid definition to include storage or demand response adds complexity requiring more study time before any expedited treatment is appropriate.
quotes: Studying only a hypothetical "net" injection or withdrawal, without considering the system effects of the hybrid load demanding up to its full gross level of demand (when, for example, its co-located generating facility is unavailable), would create unreasonable reliability risks.
it is premature to assume that the breadth of hybrid options proposed by various commenters should all be entitled to expedited interconnection study or that expedited study is feasible

letters.desc: FirstEnergy flags that the ANOPR's direct-assignment proposal covers hybrid facilities, which raises the same jurisdictional cost-allocation concerns as for pure load customers.
quotes: the ANOPR's suggestion that "load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through the interconnection studies" threatens to inhibit this goal.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy opposes studying hybrid facilities on a net basis because NERC TPL-001 requires separate loss-of-load and loss-of-generation contingency tests. Netting also under-sizes interconnection capacity when generation output exceeds load consumption.
quotes: Studying the net impact of hybrid facilities undermines the North American Electric Reliability Corporation ("NERC") transmission planning performance standards, which require testing the ability of the transmission system to withstand specific contingencies including loss of load and loss of generation.
netting fails to provide the redundant protection necessary for the system to perform reliably.

if the transmission network is only planned to support the net withdrawal and export at the point of interconnection, the interconnection capability may be undersized compared to the amount of generation that could be made available at a time when the load customer is curtailed or not consuming power.
netting raises another issue not addressed in the initial comments: it undermines NERC standards and therefore also clashes with the ANOPR's principle fourteen.

letters.org: Georgia Power CompanyAlabama Power CompanyMississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: Southern Companies argue that granting end-use customers a federal withdrawal right would circumvent state retail franchise laws and the limits Congress placed on FERC's retail jurisdiction. They urge FERC to drop or carefully narrow this concept.
quotes: An end-use customer has no right to withdraw power from the grid without being subject to applicable state laws on retail energy use and applicable retail franchises, and Congress has unambiguously kept the Commission out of the business of retail regulation, respecting states' police powers.

letters.desc: The filer opposes net-basis study for hybrid facilities, stating that studying load and generation only at net amounts masks real reliability needs and can shift costs to other customers when on-site generation goes offline.
quotes: Load is not competing with generation for access to the system and is therefore not similarly situated to generation.
on-site load and generation need to be studied at their full amounts to ensure reliable interconnection.

letters.desc: The KCC flags that ANOPR reform principle 9, which gives large load customers an option to build similar to generator interconnection customers, could be read to override state franchise rights and certificated service territories, including by allowing third-party generators to co-locate with large loads in areas served by exclusive franchisees.
quotes: This principle suggests that large load customers have a right to directly interconnect to the FERC-regulated grid that trumps state laws regarding retail choice and certificated service territories.

letters.desc: The Maryland PSC warns that netting large load against co-located generation could hide the load from grid operators and exclude it from planning scenarios, creating reliability risks that grow as large loads multiply.
quotes: netting load against generation supply at hybrid facilities could pose a risk to grid reliability. Depending on how the hybrid arrangement is configured and how it is treated by system planners, netting load against the generator's supply to the grid may risk the load: (a) escaping the "view" of grid operators during normal operations; and (b) being excluded from future planning scenarios.

letters.desc: The MISO Transmission Owners insist that co-located load and generation must be studied and metered on a gross rather than net basis for reliability and cost-allocation reasons. They oppose netting arrangements that would reduce a hybrid customer's transmission service obligations.
quotes: large load owners should only be able to co-locate and contract for power directly from generators to the extent state laws and regulations allow.  Second, it is critical to both system planning and operational awareness that load and generation are studied and metered separately, on a gross rather than a net basis.

system protection facilities do not guarantee the prevention of unauthorized injections or withdrawals.  This is one of the reasons that it is imperative from a reliability perspective that the load and generation of a hybrid facility are studied and metered separately.
the MISO Transmission Owners are concerned that the Eleventh and Twelfth Principles raise significant cost allocation concerns, as well as undue discrimination concerns

letters.desc: The filer opposes netting co-located generation against load for purposes of transmission service and ancillary service charges, contending that large load owners still rely on the grid during generator outages and should pay on a gross-load basis.
quotes: Maintaining the status quo of cost responsibility for transmission service and ancillary services will provide large load owners and transmission providers clarity and certainty and avoid preventable and unnecessary litigation.

Basing load owners' transmission service responsibilities on their withdrawal rights alone fails to account for transmission service large load owners will use during the planned and unplanned outages that generators experience, i.e., times when large load owners will benefit from the broader transmission system.

letters.org: New York Transmission OwnersCentral Hudson Gas & Electric CorporationNew York Power Authority ,New York State Electric & Gas Corp. and Rochester Gas and El ,Niagara Mohawk d/b/a/ National Grid ,Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. and Orange and ,Long Island Power Authority ,
letters.desc: The NYTOs oppose extending option-to-build rights to transmission-level network upgrades. They argue such rights are appropriate only for customer-specific radial facilities that are not relied upon for network service, where the customer assumes full NERC lifecycle responsibility and the transmission owner retains protection, switching, and operational authority at the point of interconnection.
quotes: Option-to-build authority is appropriate only for facilities used exclusively by the requesting customer and only where: (1) the facilities are not used or relied upon for network transmission service; (2) the customer assumes full lifecycle responsibility and NERC obligations if the asset qualifies as a BES facility; (3) the Transmission Owner retains authority over system protection, interconnection criteria, switching, and operational coordination at the point of interconnection; and (4) no ongoing operation and maintenance, modeling, or retrofit obligations shift to the Transmission Owner absent Section 205 cost of service recovery.

letters.org: North Carolina Utilities Commission Public Staff
letters.desc: A federal interconnection rule cannot confer a right for a large load to actually be served as a retail customer, which is reserved to the states alone.
quotes: A Commission rule prescribing the methods, timing, and transmission pricing for interconnecting load to the transmission system could not, at the end of the day, provide any right for that load to be actually served as a retail customer, a matter unquestionably reserved to the states alone.

letters.desc: ODEC opposes sizing hybrid interconnections to injection and withdrawal rights alone, arguing the grid must accommodate either the load or generation operating independently at full capacity. Limiting transmission service obligations to withdrawal rights shifts costs to other ratepayers when the generator is unavailable.
quotes: ODEC does not support studying hybrid facilities based on the injection/withdrawal rights requested because we believe it will cause issues stemming from generator outages and the retirement of load or generating facilities, as the transmission system will still need to be built to accommodate either the load or the generating facility operating independently in the future.
Any significant change to either the load or the generation should require the project to refile, ensuring that system studies remain accurate and reliable.
ODEC does not support limiting utilities serving large loads' transmission service obligation based on their withdrawal rights.

Facilities served by dedicated generation and hybrid facilities should be responsible for contributing to the upkeep and maintenance of the transmission system based on peak demand, without consideration of any co-located generation facilities.

letters.desc: OMS urges FERC to confirm that interconnection approval does not automatically grant large loads the right to self-procure from wholesale markets, limiting any such access to approved co-location or behind-the-meter arrangements.
quotes: FERC should confirm that interconnection under this framework does not confer a right to self-procure from wholesale markets, except through approved arrangements such as co-location or behind-the-meter generation used for flexibility or demand-response purposes.

letters.desc: PG&E finds the proposed hybrid study methodology flawed because it ignores the reality that generators and loads will sometimes be offline simultaneously. It calls for multi-scenario studies that cover full and partial outage conditions.
quotes: any final rule should be consistent with the Commission's determination earlier this year 'the states get to determine which entities are legally permitted to provide electricity to retail customers in co-location arrangements. The states also get to determine how the wholesale costs of providing electricity to those retail customers are recovered through retail rates.'

This aspect of the ANOPR is problematic and requires modification. This proposal does not account for the likely situation that for any given time period, a co-located generator may be off-line (requiring the load to solely utilize the transmission system) or a large load facility may be partially or completely off-line or using less energy than forecasted (resulting in the generator injecting more into the transmission system).

the Commission should direct that hybrid facilities be studied under multiple potential scenarios so that the interconnection facilities can be designed and built to accommodate the inevitable circumstance of a generator or large load being partially or wholly off-line.

letters.desc: PFT is concerned that co-location arrangements allow large loads to bypass transmission upgrade costs and network charges, reducing the generation pool available to other market participants and raising costs for existing customers.
quotes: Such arrangements potentially avoid transmission upgrade costs and network service charges while creating reliability concerns: largest customers that can satisfy their demand close to the point of generation, effectively reducing the pool of generation available to all other customers participating in markets.

letters.desc: PPL opposes netting co-located load against co-located generation when calculating transmission service charges, arguing this undercharges large loads and shifts costs to network customers.
quotes: Transmission service should not be based on a netted value with the generator, as this risks undercharging for use based on the characteristics of the generator and the load.

letters.org: Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group
letters.desc: The filer argues large load customers lack the construction experience of generator interconnection customers and should not receive the same option-to-build rights for interconnection facilities and network upgrades.
quotes: large load interconnection customers are not similarly situated to generator interconnection customers and should not be afforded the same option to build interconnection facilities and stand-alone network upgrades because they lack experience constructing or developing those facilities.

letters.desc: SPP argues that hybrid facilities must be studied on their full gross withdrawal and injection capacity, not net rights. A generator trip can expose the full load to the grid instantly, and studying only net rights would leave SPP unable to plan for that contingency. Coincident-peak billing on net rights also risks shifting costs to other consumers.
quotes: system protection facilities may not fully protect the grid from stability issues, and as such, the full load at a hybrid facility should be considered when applying a MW threshold.

SPP cannot appropriately study the actual impacts of that load on the Transmission System without studying the full impact of its potential withdrawals from the Transmission System. Although this load may have a generator capable of offsetting the load at most times, in the event that generator goes offline, SPP would have to provide the full MW amount to serve that load, and would, therefore, experience the effects of its full withdrawal even if only temporarily.

Even with system protections in place, very rapid withdrawals of large amounts of power can adversely affect the transmission grid (e.g., through rapid frequency excursions and unintended protection operations). All generators are susceptible to unexpected tripping, and protection schemes themselves may fail under fast dynamic conditions.

If the Commission mandates a transmission cost netting paradigm, which is implied by the hybrid example, consideration should also be given to the converse scenario, where a facility with 600 MW of load and 500 MW of generation has 100 MW of withdrawal rights. In this case, billing for transmission based upon coincident peak usage can be particularly problematic if the hybrid resource requires transmission to be built and maintained, yet the hybrid facility avoids the coincident peak upon which billing is currently calculated.

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU opposes allowing hybrid facilities to avoid full interconnection requirements based on net position. Studying only net injection or withdrawal understates real system impacts and lets hybrids leapfrog generators competing for the same transfer capability.
quotes: UIU opposes the contention that the hybrid facilities should not be required to meet the minimum interconnection requirements applicable to its entire load or generation.

The type of incentive promulgated in the ANOPR would distort queue prioritization, potentially allowing large loads to leapfrog generation projects competing for the same transfer capability because they are not required to financially support their full interconnection request.

letters.desc: Cost commitment mechanisms and deposit requirements should account for specific risks of hybrid interconnections and regional variations in transmission configurations.
quotes: But such commitments must be well-tailored to the specific risks posed by large loads and hybrid interconnections, and they must account for regional variations and variations in interconnection configurations.

letters.desc: APS seeks clarification on whether hybrid facilities (co-located load and generation) will be required to meet NERC frequency and ramping standards.
quotes: Will hybrid facilities be expected to match the NERC requirements?

letters.desc: ISO-NE supports studying hybrids based on net injection and withdrawal rights but notes that full interconnection studies are still needed. It also asks FERC to explain how 'withdrawal rights' fits with existing transmission service constructs.
quotes: ISO-NE is supportive of this principle, the impacts of which would be reflected in study assumptions.  ISO-NE also notes that this principle would not negate the need for Interconnection Studies.
ISO-NE respectfully submits that clarity is needed with respect to how the concept of "withdrawal rights" fits with the currently established transmission service concepts and constructs.

letters.desc: SMA notes that the highly variable load profiles of data centers present system stability challenges that must factor into how hybrid facility injection and withdrawal rights are defined and studied.
quotes: A key consideration for hybrid facilities serving large, variable loads such as data centers is the highly dynamic load profile, which can pose challenges for maintaining system stability.

letters.desc: Talen notes the ANOPR does not explain how a large load or hybrid facility could directly connect to transmission without also using facilities that qualify as distribution under the Commission's seven-factor test.
quotes: the ANOPR fails to define the term “directly” and it remains unclear how a large load or hybrid facility could directly connect to the transmission system without also connecting with facilities that qualify as distribution facilities under the Commission’s seven-factor test.
